lead: Real gas streams carry several solutes, and one solvent must take them all: each solute has its own equilibrium line, but one L/G serves every component. A reactive solvent goes further: it consumes the dissolved solute, so the liquid holds far more and the absorption rate rises by an enhancement factor. These ideas set solvent choice and column size for amine CO₂ and H₂S removal and lime SO₂ scrubbing.
prereq: You need: the absorption factor, HTU and NTU and film theory (from Film, penetration and surface renewal theories).

blocks.text: A multicomponent absorber receives a gas with solutes A, B, C and one liquid. At equilibrium each solute obeys its own Henry law: y<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>, where y<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction in the gas, x<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction in the liquid, and m<sub>i</sub> is the slope of that solute's equilibrium line. One m per solute, not one average m for the mixture.

The operating line is shared. A solute balance gives the same liquid flow L and gas flow G for every component, so L/G is one number. For component i the absorption factor is A<sub>i</sub> = L/(m<sub>i</sub>G). It is dimensionless. Large A<sub>i</sub> means easy absorption; small A<sub>i</sub> means hard absorption.

Find the key component first: the solute whose recovery is specified. Compute A<sub>i</sub> for each solute and use the Kremser equation component by component: with fresh solvent the fraction of solute i absorbed in N stages is (A<sub>i</sub><sup>N+1</sup> − A<sub>i</sub>)/(A<sub>i</sub><sup>N+1</sup> − 1). Solutes with A<sub>i</sub> well above 1 are almost fully absorbed; those with A<sub>i</sub> below 1 are absorbed only to about the fraction A<sub>i</sub>. The key component's recovery fixes L/G and N; every other solute then takes what those values give. Some syllabi teach a shortcut that handles all the components together, the Edmister group method. Never replace the individual m<sub>i</sub> by an average Henry constant.

A reactive solvent removes solute by reaction as it dissolves. Common examples are CO₂ in NaOH or amine, H₂S in amine, and SO₂ in lime slurry. The reaction keeps dissolved solute concentration low, so more gas can dissolve. Film and penetration models with reaction compare reaction rate with diffusion rate; that comparison gives the Hatta number.

blocks.where: k is the pseudo-first-order reaction rate constant (s⁻¹); D<sub>A</sub> is the solute diffusivity (m²/s); k<sub>L</sub> is the liquid-film mass transfer coefficient (m/s). Ha is dimensionless.

blocks.text: The enhancement factor E is the flux with reaction divided by the flux without reaction at the same interfacial concentration. Its size depends on Ha.

items: Slow reaction, Ha below about 0.3: reaction occurs mainly in the bulk liquid, E ≈ 1, and the rate is close to physical absorption.

Fast reaction, Ha above about 3 and much smaller than E<sub>i</sub>: reaction occurs inside the film and E ≈ Ha, so the flux is multiplied by Ha. E<sub>i</sub> is the instantaneous enhancement factor defined in the next bullet.

Instantaneous reaction: A and B meet at a sharp reaction plane inside the film. When Ha is comparable to or larger than E<sub>i</sub>, use E = E<sub>i</sub> = 1 + D<sub>B</sub>c<sub>B</sub>/(b D<sub>A</sub>c<sub>Ai</sub>), where D<sub>B</sub> is the diffusivity of the liquid reactant B (m²/s), c<sub>B</sub> its bulk concentration (kmol/m³), b the moles of B used per mole of A, D<sub>A</sub> the solute diffusivity and c<sub>Ai</sub> the interfacial solute concentration (kmol/m³).

blocks.text: Consequences: solvent capacity rises, so the liquid rate falls; for an irreversible reaction the dissolved solute exerts almost no back pressure, so the equilibrium gas mole fraction is y* ≈ 0 and the driving force y − y* ≈ y; the liquid-film resistance shrinks and the gas film may control. Figure 3.9.1 draws the film for three cases from the chapter's numbers. The film model and the penetration model give almost the same E for fast reactions, so either can be used in an exam.

For a fast reaction with y* ≈ 0, the driving force y − y* ≈ y, so the operating line has almost the full gas mole fraction as driving force. The NTU and HTU method from Chapter 3.7 still applies, but if the liquid film resistance disappears, the overall gas coefficient is close to the gas-film coefficient. The tower becomes gas-film controlled, so packing wetting and gas velocity matter more than liquid-side kinetics.

With several solutes and a reaction, each solute has its own m<sub>i</sub>, Ha<sub>i</sub> and E<sub>i</sub>: an amine may take H₂S fast and CO₂ slowly, so selectivity comes from kinetics as well as solubility.

figure.caption: Solute A in the liquid film, from the interface (left) to the bulk liquid (right). Without reaction it falls in a straight line; with a fast reaction (Ha = 3) it is used up inside the film; with an instantaneous reaction it meets reactant B at a plane, here at x/δ = 1/6 for E<sub>i</sub> = 6.

spec.aria: Plot of concentration against distance through the liquid film with a straight falling line for no reaction, a curve that drops steeply for Ha 3, a steep line for A reaching zero at one sixth of the film, and a dashed rising line for reactant B beyond that plane.

examples.question: CO₂ is absorbed into a solution in which it reacts with a pseudo-first-order rate constant k = 100 s⁻¹. The CO₂ diffusivity is D<sub>A</sub> = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, the liquid film coefficient is k<sub>L</sub> = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, and the interfacial concentration is c<sub>Ai</sub> = 0.03 kmol/m³. Find Ha, the enhancement factor, and the absorption flux. Compare with physical absorption.
steps: Write the data: k = 100 s⁻¹, D<sub>A</sub> = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, k<sub>L</sub> = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, c<sub>Ai</sub> = 0.03 kmol/m³.
Ha = 20 is well above 3. The amine is in large excess, so E<sub>i</sub> is far above 20 and the fast-reaction rule applies: E ≈ Ha = 20.
Flux with reaction = E k<sub>L</sub> c<sub>Ai</sub> = 20 × 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.03 = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s).
examples.answer: Ha = 20, E ≈ 20, and the reactive flux is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s), twenty times the physical flux of 6 × 10⁻⁷ kmol/(m²·s).
examples.check:
k = 100.0
D = 1.6e-9
kL = 2e-5
cAi = 0.03
Ha = (k * D) ** 0.5 / kL
E = Ha
flux = E * kL * cAi
physical = kL * cAi
ratio = flux / physical
print(Ha)
print(E)
print(flux)
print(physical)
print(ratio)

examples.question: A lean-oil absorber with N = 4 theoretical stages treats 100 kmol/h of gas containing 8 kmol/h ethane, 5 kmol/h propane, 3 kmol/h n-butane and 1 kmol/h n-pentane (the rest methane). Fresh oil enters at L/G = 1.0 (dilute approximation). The equilibrium slopes at column conditions are m = 3.6 (ethane), 1.25 (propane), 0.45 (n-butane) and 0.16 (n-pentane). Find the fraction and amount of each solute absorbed.
steps: Fraction absorbed φ = (A<sup>5</sup> − A)/(A<sup>5</sup> − 1), since N + 1 = 5.
Ethane: A⁵ = 0.00165; φ = (0.00165 − 0.278)/(0.00165 − 1) = 0.277, so 8 × 0.277 = 2.21 kmol/h absorbed. Almost exactly A: below 1, the limit is A.
examples.answer: Absorbed: ethane 27.7 % (2.21 kmol/h), propane 70.2 % (3.51), n-butane 97.7 % (2.93), n-pentane 99.9 % (1.00). One L/G and one N serve all four; only m<sub>i</sub> differs.

traps: Using one average Henry constant for a mixture. Each solute has its own m<sub>i</sub>, so each has its own equilibrium line.
Setting a separate L/G for each solute. One liquid and one gas flow serve every component; the key component fixes the shared L/G.

Applying E = Ha outside the fast-reaction range. E ≈ Ha is valid only when Ha is above about 3 and much smaller than E<sub>i</sub>; for slow reaction E is near 1, and when Ha is comparable to or larger than E<sub>i</sub> use E = E<sub>i</sub>.
Mixing units in Ha: k must be in s⁻¹ for pseudo-first-order reaction, D<sub>A</sub> in m²/s, and k<sub>L</sub> in m/s.
Using E<sub>i</sub> for a slow reaction; it applies only when the reaction is far faster than diffusion and B is in the liquid.

quiz.q: Define the enhancement factor E in absorption with chemical reaction.
quiz.a: E = flux with reaction divided by flux without reaction at the same interfacial concentration and liquid flow. It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why is L/G a single value in a multicomponent absorber?
quiz.a: All solutes share the same liquid and gas streams. A solute balance gives one L and one G, so L/G is fixed for the column; only m<sub>i</sub> and A<sub>i</sub> differ from solute to solute.

quiz.q: For k = 50 s⁻¹, D<sub>A</sub> = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, and k<sub>L</sub> = 3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, find Ha.
A reacting system gives Ha = 0.5. Explain whether E ≈ Ha is a good estimate.
quiz.a: No. Ha = 0.5 is not in the fast-reaction range. E ≈ Ha needs Ha above about 3. At 0.5 the reaction is largely in the bulk liquid and E is closer to 1; using 0.5 would understate the flux.

quiz.q: For an instantaneous reaction, D<sub>B</sub> = D<sub>A</sub>, b = 1, c<sub>B</sub> = 0.1 kmol/m³ and c<sub>Ai</sub> = 0.02 kmol/m³. Find E<sub>i</sub>.
quiz.a: E<sub>i</sub> = 1 + D<sub>B</sub>c<sub>B</sub>/(b D<sub>A</sub>c<sub>Ai</sub>) = 1 + (1 × 0.1)/(1 × 0.02) = 1 + 5 = 6. In film theory the reaction plane then sits at x/δ = 1/6.

quiz.q: Explain two design consequences of a fast reaction with E much greater than 1.
quiz.a: Solvent capacity rises, so the liquid rate can fall. The equilibrium back pressure is nearly zero, so y<sup>*</sup> ≈ 0 and the driving force is y − y<sup>*</sup> ≈ y. Liquid-film resistance shrinks, so the gas film may control and the tower becomes gas-film controlled.

quiz.q: In the lean-oil example, what L/G would give propane A = 1.25 with the same m, and what fraction of propane would 4 stages then absorb?

beyond: Not for the exam. In amine CO₂ capture the Hatta number and enhancement factor decide the packing height, and rate-based simulators solve the film equations with reaction. Search "Hatta number", "enhancement factor" and "rate-based absorption".
